extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; playwrights, actors, preachers, authors, and genteel readers interested in taste, manners, and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Extract prescriptive norms and evaluative standards embedded in a Spectator issue (1711) covering preaching, theatrical writing/acting, literary style, social etiquette, and letters on love — i.e., guidance for authors, actors, preachers, and polite society about propriety and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and directness in preaching and public speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers and preachers ought to 'enter into the Matter' rather than load discourse with circumstantial citations and prolix authorities (mocked example: the man who, instead of coming to the point, prefaced with citations from Tillotson and Beveridge and 'briefly explain' but did not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive circumstantiality and over-reliance on authorities; do not substitute long lists of citations or pedantic exactness for clear, direct exposition. The essay notes this is particularly burdensome when such 'Genius' is in authority (e.g., a preacher who reads too much and will not trust his own parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frivolous disputation and needless scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not raise hair-splitting arguments about matters universally conceded (examples: putting someone to prove that Snow is white; disputing trivial points of time and place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert small knowledge into perpetual, unanswerable doubts. Such impertinent disputation 'turns what little Knowledge they have into a ready Capacity of raising Doubts' and makes interlocutors frivolous and unanswerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony of the snuff-box (etiquette of offering snuff)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are rules for offering snuff to a stranger, a friend, or a mistress, 'according to the Degrees of Familiarity or Distance', with distinct gestures (the Careless, the Scornful, the Politick, and the Surly Pinch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer snuff with attention to social distance and appropriate gesture; the advertisement promises instruction and training in these ceremonies, treating snuff-box manners as codified social conduct (presented as an alternative to fan culture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of glory (Tully's three particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tully's account: the perfection of glory consists in (1) that the people love us, (2) that they have confidence in us, (3) that they think we deserve honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging 'greatness' or fame in a commonwealth (and by extension public reputation), assess popular affection, public confidence, and the sense that honour is deserved. The essay adds that under a monarchy one must also consider the Prince's favour: a favourite should be popular because a favourite and a favourite because popular.

rubrics_metrics.name: True glory vs empty/ostentatious glory
rubrics_metrics.description: True glory arises from virtue, personal labour, knowledge, and application to useful arts (exemplified by Peter the Great); empty glory arises from ostentation, spreading fame through territory, luxury, and the corruption that accompanies it (exemplified by Lewis of France).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rulers and public figures by whether fame is built on virtuous, lasting achievements (education, public improvement, personal example) versus superficial displays (statues, equipage, conquest for fame). The essay warns that 'Glory is nothing else but the Shadow of Virtue' and disappears when virtue departs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting must be proper, graceful, and precise (theatrical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: In theatrical speaking, if the performer is not exactly proper and graceful, he is 'utterly ridiculous'; merely performing the part is not commendable, and the least deviation is contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors should cultivate exactness and grace; theatrical performance (which primarily pleases ears and eyes) cannot tolerate slovenliness. The author contrasts this with public speaking of weightier matters, where substance may compensate for awkward delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep corporeal stunts separate from legitimate drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Rope-dancers, tumblers, and extravagant bodily feats suited the Bear-Garden and should be dismissed from the regular stage; the mixing of corporeal and intellectual acting is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import acrobatics and dangerous physical spectacles into the regular theatre where intellectual/representational acting is expected. Such stunts degrade theatrical standards and confuse audiences whose expectations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriateness of subject matter (no witches in comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements like witchcraft and solemn incantations are proper machines for tragedy (as in Macbeth) but are 'extremely foreign' to the business of comedy; transplanting horror into comedy is a misapplication of subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should choose subject matter suited to their genre; imitation of Shakespeare's darker devices in comic contexts is an error. The Lancashire Witches is criticised for using tragical machinery in a comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecent, immodest, or tasteless jests in plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Jests that raise the loudest mirth yet are 'painful to right Sense' and 'an Outrage upon Modesty' betray poor taste; poets should not sacrifice the best part of their audience to the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should aim to please the 'People of the best Understanding' and not pander to low tastes (e.g., sexual indecencies or coarse jokes) that win cheap applause but offend decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not excuse immoral conduct by facile moralizing (theatrical morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays that conclude by dismissing immoral actions with a remark like 'Design what we will, There is a Fate which over-rules us still' improperly absolve guilt (example: marriage without parental consent justified by fate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic endings should not trivialize or morally excuse wrongdoing; playwrights must be cautious about the morals they leave audiences with and avoid loose reconciliations that excuse vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style: prefer naturalness, propriety, and clarity over quaint points
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators of Milton or advocates of 'Point, or Turn' err by valuing uncouth/antique words, forced antithesis, and quaint allusion above 'what is Just, Proper and Natural'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should avoid mistaking 'point' or over-wrought wit for genuine excellence; beware luxuriance of fancy that creates blemishes. Aim for naturalness, grace, and clarity rather than artificial conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct in company: manage one's humour before imposing it on others
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is a troublesome companion to himself (imposing sullenness or ill humour) will not be agreeable to others; one should 'reason themselves into good-humour, before they impose themselves upon their Friends'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use drinking or company to remove humours that you yourself create; cultivate good temper internally before socialising so as not to burden companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour at gaming: lose with grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Female gamesters (and players generally) should not be 'Transmigrated into the veriest Wasps' at the card table; they should be instructed 'to lose with a better Grace'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of polite behaviour is bearing defeat gracefully; authors and social critics should counsel temperance and decorum at gaming tables so as not to shame oneself or disturb company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love-letter and married conduct: piety, constancy, modesty, and mutual improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Good love-letters and enduring marital affection display vigilance for the beloved's welfare, piety, modesty, steady attention, gratitude, and ongoing endeavour to improve for one another (illustrated by a set of letters across forty years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model romantic expression on devotion, religion, modesty, and long-term constancy rather than romantic ranting or fantastical 'Romantick' behaviour; letters should combine tenderness with moral seriousness and mutual edification.
